tpStops: Thuan Phuoc Bridge is the last crossing on the Han River before Da Nang Bay, about 1,856 m long.
The aerodynamic steel box girder is welded from 69 segments; 27 m of clearance lets ships into the bay.
Two reinforced-concrete towers rise 80 m above their bases, with crossbeams at the top and beneath the deck.
The two 360 mm main cables pass over saddles; an aviation light blinks on each tower.
Twelve 50 m prestressed-concrete spans on each side slope down to Nguyen Tat Thanh Street and the Son Tra peninsula.
Son Tra peninsula lies to the east; 114 hangers about 9.9 m apart tie the main cables to the girder.
At night LEDs on the cables, hangers and towers shift through blue, purple, pink and green, flowing along the bridge like wind heading out to sea.
shStops: Opened on 29 March 2000, the 487.7 m Han River Bridge links Le Duan Street with Pham Van Dong Street.
The 122.7 m centre span rotates 90° around a round pier. The tour swings the bridge once at 30× speed.
The swing span rests on a rail ring and rollers around the pier; a king pin keeps it centred as it turns.
When open, the span lies along the river, leaving two channels for ships on either side of the pier.
Before swinging, the signals turn red and barriers drop at both ends of the span; vehicles already on it drive off.
Its mast is taller than the ~11 m clearance, so it can only pass when the bridge is open. In real life the bridge swings at 23:00 on Saturday and Sunday nights.
ttlStops: A sail on the Han River
The 731 m Tran Thi Ly Bridge has a single pylon leaning west like a sail filled with wind.
The 145 m concrete pylon rises 134 m above the deck and leans away from the 230 m main span to balance the pull of the cables.
Instead of being fixed to the pier, the pylon stands on two steel bearings, each carrying about 250,000 kN.
At night LEDs on the pylon, cables and deck shift through red, pink, purple and blue.
A single semi-fan plane on the centreline anchors in the 5.5 m median of the main span; the 34.5 m deck carries six lanes.
In the two rear planes the highest cable anchors nearest the pylon and the lowest farthest away, forming a hyperbolic surface seen from below.
Just to the north is the old steel truss bridge, now for pedestrians only.

stops: The 666 m Dragon Bridge links downtown Hai Chau (west bank) with Son Tra district and My Khe Beach (east bank).
A curling tail with flared fins at the west end, facing the city centre.
Six traffic lanes, three each way; a 6 m central median; 2.5 m sidewalks on both sides. 37.5 m wide in total.
The dragon’s body rises highest over the central span. Steel hangers tie its belly to the deck.
Five main spans rest on piers in the riverbed; tour boats pass beneath.
The head faces the sea. At 21:00 on Saturday and Sunday nights the dragon breathes fire, then sprays water.
A 731 m cable-stayed bridge with a single 145 m pylon leaning 12°; its three cable planes form a sail filled with wind.
Seen from the river mouth. Son Tra Mountain lies to the northeast, the Hai Van range to the northwest.

hrNote: Proposal of 2025, investment planned 2031–2045, total 6,880 billion VND. Cross-section, depths and portal architecture are estimates.
hrStops: The 2025 proposal is a tunnel of about 1,670 m linking Dong Da (Hai Chau) with Van Don (Son Tra): a 600 m immersed tunnel under the river, 380 m of cut-and-cover on the banks and 415 m of open ramps. Investment is planned for 2031–2045.
Next to Dien Hai Citadel the portal is kept low and clad in old-brick tones. An 80 m louvre roof cuts glare as cars enter from harsh sun, keeps out driving rain and lets typhoon wind pass through.
Da Nang often floods when heavy rain meets high tide. The road crest before the portal is raised 1 m above the street, with a sliding flood gate to hold the water back.

Five immersed elements of 120 m each lie about 6 m below the riverbed level, with at least 1 m of cover above the roof. On each bank comes cut-and-cover with diaphragm walls, then open ramps no steeper than 4.5%.

Each element is cast in a dry dock, sealed at both ends and towed out; ballast water sinks it into the dredged trench. Jacks pull it tight against its neighbour and a rubber GINA gasket seals the joint.
Three lanes each way: two car lanes at 60 km/h and a motorbike lane on the right. Jet fans ventilate along the tunnel, and the entrance zone is lit brighter so eyes can adapt.
Between the two tubes runs a pressurised, smoke-free corridor. A green cross-passage door every 100 m leads into it, with SOS boxes and extinguishers every 50 m.
On the Son Tra side the portal recalls sea waves and fishing villages, with basket boats beside it. The planned investment of 6,880 billion VND would relieve the Dragon and Han River bridges.

allStops: A journey across four bridges
From Tran Thi Ly Bridge we follow the Han River north past Dragon Bridge and Han River Bridge to Thuan Phuoc Bridge.
12° leaning pylon
Tran Thi Ly Bridge is 731 m long, with a single 145 m pylon leaning west like a sail in the wind.
Looking back from the north
Three planes of stay cables fan out from the pylon; beside it is the old Nguyen Van Troi Bridge, now for pedestrians.
Down the Han River
About 1.3 km to Dragon Bridge; Hai Chau city centre on the west bank, Son Tra district on the east.
Dragon Bridge
666 m long with 6 lanes; the steel dragon winds over five arch spans, the main one 200 m.
Dragon head
The head faces the sea. On Saturday and Sunday at 9 pm the dragon breathes fire, then water.
Heading north
About 1.1 km further downstream is the Han River Bridge.
Han River Bridge
Vietnam's only swing bridge, opened on 29 March 2000. Its 122.7 m centre span is about to turn 90° (30× speed).
Swing span open
When open, the span lies along the river, leaving two channels for ships. In real life it swings at 11 pm on Saturdays and Sundays.
Proposed tunnel route
Below lies the route of the Han River tunnel — a proposed option, not yet built.
Thuan Phuoc Bridge
The last bridge on the Han River, about 1,856 m long; its 405 m main span hangs from two main cables.
Tower saddle
Two H-shaped towers 80 m tall; the two Ø360 mm main cables pass over saddles at the top.
Han River mouth
The Han River flows into Da Nang Bay. The journey ends here — drag the mouse to explore on your own.

swStops: Asia Park, on the west bank of the Han River, over 2 km south of Dragon Bridge. 115 m tall, 64 cabins.
Foot of the wheel and the station
The station base has three arches, where passengers board. 64 cabins × 6 passengers, about 15 minutes per turn.
It began as Igosu 108 at Biwako Tower (Shiga, Japan, 1992), was moved to Da Nang and opened on 18 July 2014. Some sources report it closed in September 2025; the model shows it in operation.
Into a cabin, up to the top
In real life the ride to the top takes about 7.5 minutes; the model fast-forwards. Cabins hang outside the rim, so they stay upright.
From about 115 m up, to the north lie Tran Thi Ly Bridge (nearest, about 1 km), then Dragon Bridge, Han River Bridge and, far away, Thuan Phuoc Bridge.
About 13,000 LEDs on 32 main spokes change colour in each show style, with red-rimmed cabins. The journey ends here.
